stem: A 52-year-old man comes to the office due to increasing puffiness of his face over the past 2 weeks.  He has had no leg swelling, dyspnea, rash, or itching but has had a persistent cough for the last several weeks.  The patient says, "I haven't been coughing up phlegm, but sometimes I notice some blood on the tissue when I cough particularly hard."  He has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes daily for the past 30 years.  The patient works as a welder on an assembly line.  Physical examination shows swelling involving the right face and arm.  There is engorgement of subcutaneous veins on the right side of the neck.  Left face and upper extremity appear normal.  Lung auscultation demonstrates scattered rhonchi.  There is no ascites or pedal edema.  Occlusion of which of the following veins is the most likely cause of this patient's swelling?​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌
explanation:
This patient's unilateral face and arm swelling is most likely due to an obstructed right brachiocephalic (innominate) vein.  This most commonly occurs due to external venous compression by an apical lung cancer (as suggested by cough and hemoptysis).  Less commonly, thrombotic occlusion of the brachiocephalic vein can develop as a complication of an indwelling central venous catheter.

The subclavian vein drains blood from the arm and is met by the external jugular vein draining blood from the ipsilateral side of the face.  Just proximal to the union with the external jugular vein, the subclavian vein is met by the internal jugular vein (which drains blood from the brain and portions of the face and neck) to form the brachiocephalic vein.  Therefore, right brachiocephalic vein obstruction causes redness and edema of the right arm and right side of the face.

More commonly than brachiocephalic obstruction of either side, an apical lung tumor causes obstruction of the superior vena cava (SVC) and leads to SVC syndrome.  In SVC syndrome, redness and edema of the bilateral arms and face is expected (Choice E).  In addition, total obstruction of blood drainage from the brain can cause cerebral edema and confusion (and ultimately death).

(Choice A)  The axillary vein is formed by the union of the basilic and brachial veins and more proximally forms the subclavian vein when met by the cephalic vein.  Obstruction of the axillary vein causes redness and edema of the ipsilateral arm but does not affect the face.

(Choices C and D)  Obstruction of either the external or internal jugular vein can cause redness and edema of the face but does not affect the arm.

Educational objective:The brachiocephalic vein drains the ipsilateral jugular veins (draining blood from the face and head) and subclavian vein (draining blood from the arm).  The bilateral brachiocephalic veins combine to form the superior vena cava (SVC).  Brachiocephalic vein obstruction causes symptoms similar to those seen in SVC syndrome but on only one side of the body.​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌
